description: Bake a 9x5 loaf recipe in an 8x4 loaf pan instead. The smaller pan holds 4 cups against 8, so halve the batter and keep the same bake time, with the table.

steps: Write down the recipe batter: 5 cups.
5 x 0.5 = 2.5 cups in the 8x4 loaf pan.
The depth is unchanged, so the bake time stays 60 minutes.

faqs.answer: Volume is length times width times depth, and the small pan loses on all three: an inch shorter, an inch narrower, and a quarter inch shallower. It adds up to half the volume, 4 cups against 8.
faqs.question: Why is it half when the pans look the same size?

faqs.answer: Both can be, for different pans. Some 8x4 pans are deeper than the standard 2.5 inches and hold 5 or 6 cups. The most-cited figure is 4 cups. Measure your own pan with water, a cup at a time to the rim, and use that number.
faqs.question: My chart says the 8x4 holds 6 cups. Which is right?

faqs.answer: Beat the egg in a small cup until the yolk and white are mixed, then use half by volume. A large egg is about 3 tablespoons, so half is about 1.5 tablespoons. Save the rest for scrambled eggs.
faqs.question: How do I halve an egg?

faqs.answer: Bake it now, as a second small loaf or as muffins. Batter with baking powder or soda loses its lift sitting around, and a batter baked hours later rises poorly. A second loaf freezes well once baked and cooled.
faqs.question: Can I bake the other half later?

faqs.answer: No. The batter sits at the same depth in both pans, because the volume halved along with the pan. Same depth means the same bake time at the same temperature.
faqs.question: Does the small loaf bake faster?

felicityNote: The 8x4 pan is the half-recipe pan. One loaf for now, one for the freezer, and the recipe card stays the same.

formula.text: New batter = recipe batter x 0.5. Factor = new volume divided by old volume = 4 divided by 8 = 0.5.

howToSteps.name: Work out the factor
howToSteps.text: An 8x4 loaf pan holds 4 cups and a 9x5 holds 8. Divide 4 by 8 and the factor is 0.5. Halve the recipe.

howToSteps.name: Halve every ingredient
howToSteps.text: Halve each ingredient, including the leavening. For eggs, beat the egg and use half by volume, about 1.5 tablespoons per large egg.

howToSteps.name: Check the fill
howToSteps.text: Pour the halved batter into a greased 8x4 loaf pan. It should sit no higher than two-thirds full, about 2.7 cups.

howToSteps.name: Bake as the recipe says
howToSteps.text: Same oven temperature, same bake time. Test the center with a skewer at the recipe time.

lede: A 9x5 loaf pan holds 8 cups and an 8x4 holds 4, so the smaller pan takes exactly half the batter. The batter sits at the same depth in both, so the bake time stays the same.

title: 9x5 Loaf Pan to 8x4 Loaf Converter
tutorial: The two loaf pans look nearly identical on the shelf, and one holds twice the batter of the other. A 9x5 loaf pan holds 8 cups. An 8x4 loaf pan holds 4 cups. The factor is 4 divided by 8, which is 0.5: halve the recipe. A loaf recipe that makes 5 cups of batter becomes 2.5 cups in the small pan.

Area maths would say something different, and it would be wrong. The floors are 45 square inches against 32, a ratio of 0.71. But loaf pans taper toward the base and the 8x4 is shallower too, about 2.5 inches deep against 2.75, so the measured volumes are what count: 4 cups against 8. This swap runs on volume, measured in cups, not on floor area.

One honest note: some charts list the 8x4 loaf pan at 5 or 6 cups. Those are deeper pans with the same footprint, and they exist. The most-cited figure, measured in home kitchens and listed by Sally's Baking Addiction, Preppy Kitchen, and CooksInfo, is 4 cups. If your 8x4 looks deep, measure it yourself: fill it with water a cup at a time to the rim and count. That number is the truth for your pan.

Halving a loaf recipe means halving the eggs, which is the one fiddly part. Beat the egg in a small cup and use half by volume, about 1.5 tablespoons for a large egg. The rest of the halving is easy: half the flour, half the sugar, half the baking powder. Leavening halves like everything else.

Bake at the same temperature and the same time. The batter sits at the same depth in both pans, because the volume halved along with the pan, so the middle sets on the same schedule. The other half of the batter bakes into a second small loaf or a batch of muffins, and a loaf in the freezer is next week's breakfast sorted.
